steps.body: Zeros added to the **right end** of a decimal change nothing: 0.5, 0.50, and 0.500 are the same value. Each extra zero just says "and no more of the next smaller piece." Half a whole is half whether you write one place or three.

widget.prompt: Which statement about 0.5 and 0.50 is true?

options.label: They are equal
options.feedback: The trailing zero adds no value: 0.5 and 0.50 are the same amount.

options.label: 0.50 is bigger — it has more digits
options.feedback: Extra trailing zeros don't add size. 0.50 is just 0.5 with an empty hundredths place: equal.

options.label: 0.5 is bigger — it's simpler
options.feedback: Fewer digits doesn't mean bigger either. The trailing zero changes nothing: they're equal.

hints: Read 0.50 as 'five tenths and zero hundredths.'
explanationVariants: 0.50 is 0.5 plus an empty hundredths place — equal.
Trailing zeros never change a decimal's value.

options.label: No — that zero moved the 5 to a smaller place

predict.reveal: A zero BETWEEN the point and the digit shoves the 5 into the hundredths — ten times smaller. Where a zero sits decides whether it matters at all.

explanationVariants: Writing 0.4 as 0.40 lets you line it up with 0.40 exactly — still equal.
Padding with trailing zeros makes lengths match without changing value.

options.label: All three are equal
options.feedback: Only trailing zeros differ, so all three are the same value.

options.label: 0.400 is the biggest
options.feedback: The trailing zeros in 0.400 add nothing. All three equal 0.4.

options.label: 0.4 is the biggest
options.feedback: Length, long or short, doesn't change value here. All three are equal.

steps.body: Padding is a **tool**: give two decimals the same number of places, then compare like whole numbers. To check 0.5 against 0.45, pad to 0.50 — now compare 50 and 45. So **0.5 is greater than 0.45**, even though 0.45 has more digits.

explanationVariants: Pad 0.5 to 0.50, then compare 50 vs 45 — 0.5 wins.

choices.feedback: The extra digit is the trap. Pad 0.5 to 0.50: 50 beats 45, so 0.5 is greater.
Pad 0.5 to 0.50 and compare: 50 vs 45 — the hundredths differ, so they aren't equal.
Pad to 0.50 and compare 50 vs 45 — 0.5 is greater, despite fewer digits.

widget.successFeedback: Pad to 0.50 and compare 50 vs 45 — 0.5 is greater, despite fewer digits.
widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect at least 1 base-ten stage before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the aligned place-value model and the inspected stages.

steps.body: One caution before you go: this freedom is only for zeros on the **right end**. A zero right after the point fills the tenths place and shrinks everything. Test it —
explanationVariants: 0.05 puts a 0 in tenths, pushing the 5 down to hundredths — ten times smaller than 0.5.
A zero after the point shifts value; a zero on the right end does not.

options.label: No — 0.05 is ten times smaller
options.feedback: The 0 in 0.05 fills the tenths place, pushing the 5 to hundredths — ten times smaller than 0.5.

options.label: Yes — the zero doesn't matter
options.feedback: This zero is after the point, not on the right end. It fills tenths and shrinks the value: 0.05 is ten times smaller.

options.label: Yes — both have a 5
options.feedback: Same digit, different place. In 0.05 the 5 is in hundredths, so 0.05 is ten times smaller than 0.5.

hints: Trailing zeros (right end) keep the value; a zero right after the point changes it.
0.60 and 0.600 are 0.6 with empty places — equal.
0.06 puts the 6 in hundredths — not equal to 0.6.
explanationVariants: 0.60 and 0.600 equal 0.6 (trailing zeros); 0.06 does not (the 6 drops to hundredths).
Two of the three match 0.6 — only 0.06 differs, because its zero is after the point.

widget.prompt: Of these three — 0.60, 0.06, 0.600 — how many equal 0.6?

commonErrors.feedback: 0.06 is the odd one out — its zero is after the point, dropping the 6 to hundredths. Only 0.60 and 0.600 equal 0.6: that's 2.
Both 0.60 and 0.600 equal 0.6 (trailing zeros are free). That's 2, not 1 — 0.06 is the only mismatch.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Trailing zeros keep the value (0.60, 0.600); a zero after the point (0.06) changes it.

steps.body: Right-end zeros are free; position isn't.
takeaways: Trailing zeros on the right end don't change value: 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500.
Pad decimals to equal length, then compare like whole numbers.
A zero right after the point is different — it shrinks the value (0.5 ≠ 0.05).

concept.body: Quick rewind. **A zero added to the right end of a decimal doesn't change its value.** 0.3 = 0.30 = 0.300, because each extra zero just marks an empty smaller place. It's a handy way to make two decimals the same length before comparing.

explanationVariants: 0.30 is 0.3 with an empty hundredths place — equal.

options.label: Yes — they're equal
options.feedback: The trailing zero adds no value: 0.3 = 0.30.

options.label: No — 0.30 is bigger
options.feedback: The extra zero is on the right end, so it adds nothing. They're equal.

options.label: No — 0.3 is bigger
options.feedback: Trailing zeros don't change value in either direction. 0.3 = 0.30.
